greyLiterature.title: Guidelines for Sewerage Systems: Sewerage System Overflows (National Water Quality Management Strategy)
greyLiterature.organization: Natural Resource Management Ministerial Council (NRMMC), Australian Government
greyLiterature.summary: Australia's national guideline for managing the health and environmental impacts of sewer overflows. It lists the causes of overflows (blockages, pumping stations, infiltration/inflow, system growth, system condition), sets out regulatory and asset-management approaches, and describes short- and long-term overflow abatement plans, monitoring and emergency response. Cited by Ninh et al. (2025).
keyTakeaways: Names system growth as a cause of overflows: sewers and pumping stations too small for new subdivisions when growth is not foreseen.
Says sewer problems can hold back new development until capacity is increased.
Overflow abatement plans should use flow monitoring and hydraulic modelling, and report outcomes such as flows and overflow frequency.

steps.citation: Natural Resource Management Ministerial Council (2004). Guidelines for Sewerage Systems: Sewerage System Overflows. National Water Quality Management Strategy, Canberra.
steps.intro: A national guideline written because sewer overflows harm public health, the environment and amenity, and practice differed between states and territories.
steps.methods: A policy and practice guideline: causes and impacts of overflows, a management framework (integrated catchment management, ecologically sustainable development), regulatory approaches (presumption, demonstration, prohibition, best practice) and an overflow abatement planning process.
steps.scope: Whole sewerage systems in Australia, excluding internal building plumbing.
steps.usefulness: The Australian reference for why overflows matter and how utilities are expected to manage them. Its list of causes includes growth, which is our use case.
steps.limitations: From 2004 and general; it does not say where to place sensors. The PDF is a scan, so some text extraction is imperfect.
steps.conclusions: Utilities should run overflow abatement programs combining monitoring, modelling, maintenance, upgrades and emergency response, agreed with the regulator.
steps.reflection: Supports the business case for SA Water: growth-driven overcapacity is a recognised national overflow cause, and monitoring is part of the expected abatement plan.

greyLiterature.title: Report to Congress: Impacts and Control of CSOs and SSOs (EPA 833-R-04-001)
greyLiterature.organization: US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA)
greyLiterature.summary: EPA's national report on combined sewer overflows (CSOs) and sanitary sewer overflows (SSOs): how often they occur, their causes, their health and environmental impacts, and the money and technology used to control them. Cited by Malek Mohammadi et al. (2020).
keyTakeaways: EPA estimates 23,000–75,000 SSOs a year in the US, releasing 3–10 billion gallons of untreated wastewater; CSOs release about 850 billion gallons a year.
Of SSO events with a known cause, 48% were from full or partial blockages and 26% from wet weather and infiltration/inflow.
Most SSO events come from blockages, but most SSO volume comes from wet weather and excessive infiltration/inflow.

steps.citation: US EPA (2004). Report to Congress: Impacts and Control of CSOs and SSOs. EPA 833-R-04-001, Office of Water, Washington, DC.
steps.intro: Required by Congress to describe the extent, impacts and control of combined and sanitary sewer overflows across the United States.
steps.methods: National data compilation: EPA's SSO data management system, the Clean Watersheds Needs Survey, permits and case studies, with analysis of causes, volumes and impacts.
steps.scope: United States combined and separate sanitary sewer systems.
steps.usefulness: Gives the scale of the overflow problem and the split between blockage-driven events and wet-weather-driven volume.
steps.limitations: US data from the early 2000s; reporting differs between communities, and EPA notes small blockage overflows are likely under-reported elsewhere.
steps.conclusions: Overflows are widespread; blockages cause most events and wet weather causes most volume, so control needs both maintenance and capacity measures.
steps.reflection: Supports separating blockage and capacity mechanisms, as Vineeth asked in Meeting 3. Our growth case is a capacity problem made worse in wet weather.

greyLiterature.title: White Paper on Condition Assessment of Wastewater Collection Systems (EPA/600/R-09/049)
greyLiterature.organization: US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA)
greyLiterature.summary: EPA review of condition assessment technology for sewers: pipe failure mechanisms, defect types, CCTV and emerging inspection methods, and a summary of EPA's 2008 Technology Forum. Part of EPA's 'Innovation and Research for Water Infrastructure for the 21st Century' program (2007). Cited by Lundberg et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: Condition assessment supplies the physical condition, remaining service life and asset value needed for asset management.
Defects are classified with a standard coding system, then pipe condition is graded systematically.
Reviews wireless and remote-sensing monitoring from other industries for use in sewers.

steps.citation: US EPA (2009). White Paper on Condition Assessment of Wastewater Collection Systems. EPA/600/R-09/049, Office of Research and Development, Cincinnati, OH.
steps.intro: One of the first outputs of EPA Task Order 59 under the 2007 research program on aging water infrastructure.
steps.scope: Wastewater collection systems in the US; inspection and condition-assessment technologies.
steps.usefulness: Background on pipe-condition data (CCTV grades) that feeds the pipe-attribute risk weights.
steps.limitations: Focuses on structural condition, not hydraulic capacity or growth; technology status is as of 2009.
steps.conclusions: Utilities need consistent condition coding and better inspection technology to plan renewal.
steps.reflection: Relevant to the risk-weighting work (osp_risk.js) and to Vineeth's point that blockage history can be a weighting parameter, not the core model.

greyLiterature.title: SSOAP: A USEPA Toolbox for Sanitary Sewer Overflow Analysis and Control Planning
greyLiterature.organization: US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) and Camp Dresser & McKee
greyLiterature.summary: Describes EPA's public-domain SSOAP Toolbox for analysing rainfall-derived infiltration and inflow (RDII), running sewer capacity analyses and building SSO control plans, developed with Camp Dresser & McKee. Cited by Yong et al. (2024). Companion to EPA/600/R-07/111 and EPA/600/R-08/010, already in the library.
keyTakeaways: Between one-third and two-thirds of US sanitary sewer systems have SSO or excessive peak-flow problems.
Estimated US cost to mitigate SSOs over 20 years: $164 billion (2007 dollars) for zero overflows, $119 billion for one and $96 billion for two overflows per year per municipality.
The toolbox links RDII analysis to SWMM-based capacity assessment and control planning.

steps.citation: Vallabhaneni, S., Lai, F. H., Chan, C., Burgess, E. H. & Field, R. (2008). SSOAP – a USEPA toolbox for SSO analysis and control planning. World Environmental and Water Resources Congress 2008, ASCE.
steps.intro: EPA needed proven, public tools to characterise RDII and develop SSO control plans.
steps.methods: A cooperative research agreement (2002) with CDM produced the toolbox and a technical guide.
steps.scope: Separate sanitary sewer systems in the US.
steps.usefulness: Shows how capacity analysis and RDII are handled in practice, with costed targets per overflow level.
steps.limitations: A conference paper describing software; US cost figures.
steps.conclusions: Communities can use the toolbox to quantify RDII, assess capacity and plan SSO controls.
steps.reflection: Matches our wet-weather scenario. The cost-per-overflow-target figures are useful for the business case (D7).

greyLiterature.title: Storm Water Management Model User's Manual Version 5.0 (EPA/600/R-05/040)
greyLiterature.organization: US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA)
greyLiterature.summary: The user's manual for EPA SWMM 5.0 by L. A. Rossman: how to build, run and read SWMM models (hydrology, hydraulics and water quality). Cited by Crowley et al. (2025). Complements the SWMM Reference Manuals already in the library.
keyTakeaways: Primary documentation for the SWMM engine behind the team's Sim 2.5 growth simulation.
Covers input objects (junctions, conduits, pumps, outfalls), dry-weather inflows and RDII, and simulation options.
Revised July 2010.

greyLiterature.title: An Evaluation of Condition Assessment Protocols for Sewer Management (Client Report B-5123.6)
greyLiterature.organization: National Research Council Canada (NRC), Institute for Research in Construction
greyLiterature.summary: Compares the UK WRc sewer condition protocol with NRC guidelines and protocols used by Canadian municipalities: defect codes, deduct values, condition grades and priority rankings. Includes a survey of municipalities. Cited by Malek Mohammadi et al. (2020) and Lundberg et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: Sewer condition protocols are inconsistent in defect coding, deduct values and grading.
Maintenance priority depends on criticality and consequence of failure, not condition alone.
Calls for one integrated, consistent protocol to prioritise repair and renewal.

steps.citation: Rahman, S. & Vanier, D. J. (2004). An evaluation of condition assessment protocols for sewer management. Client Report B-5123.6, NRC Institute for Research in Construction, Ottawa.
steps.intro: Canadian municipalities used different condition protocols, making results hard to compare.
steps.methods: Protocol comparison plus a municipal survey.
steps.scope: WRc, NRC and Canadian municipal protocols.
steps.usefulness: Explains why condition data from different utilities cannot be pooled directly, which matters when borrowing factor weights from other studies.
steps.conclusions: An integrated, consistent protocol is needed.
steps.reflection: Supports our choice to borrow factor ordering but not thresholds from overseas condition models.

greyLiterature.title: Guidelines for Condition Assessment and Rehabilitation of Large Sewers
greyLiterature.organization: National Research Council Canada (NRC), Institute for Research in Construction
greyLiterature.summary: NRC guidelines, developed with 10 municipalities and two consultancies, for impact assessment, condition assessment and rehabilitation of large sewers (>900 mm) and access holes. The attached PDF is the NRC companion paper (McDonald & Zhao, NRCC-44696, 2001) summarising the guidelines; the full guideline is not openly available. Cited by Lundberg et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: Gives a consistent approach for assessing the impact of pipe failure, coding defects and prioritising rehabilitation.
Unified terminology and defect coding let utilities pool scarce condition data.
Covers access holes as well as pipes.

greyLiterature.title: Investment Needs and Future Costs of Municipal Water and Wastewater 2022–2040 (Report R2023-02)
greyLiterature.organization: Svenskt Vatten (Swedish Water & Wastewater Association)
greyLiterature.summary: Swedish industry association report (in Swedish) estimating the investment needed in municipal water and wastewater to 2040 and the effect on tariffs. Cited by Lundberg et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: Annual investment need is about SEK 31 billion against actual investment of about SEK 20–21 billion: a recurring shortfall of about SEK 10 billion a year.
About SEK 560 billion is needed up to 2040; about SEK 17 billion a year is for pipe networks.
Renewal of existing infrastructure is a large share of the need.

greyLiterature.title: Pipe Material in Swedish Water and Sewer Pipelines: Characteristics and Life-Time Expectations (SVU Report 2011-14)
greyLiterature.organization: Svenskt Vatten Utveckling (Swedish Water & Wastewater Association)
greyLiterature.summary: Malm et al. compile the properties, strengths, weaknesses and expected lifetimes of water and sewer pipe materials in Sweden (in Swedish, English summary). Cited by Lundberg et al. (2026), whose reference gives the report number as 2021-14; the correct number is 2011-14.
keyTakeaways: Sewer materials covered: concrete, PE, PVC, PP, GRP, double-wall corrugated and ceramic (vitrified clay) pipes.
Pipe life depends on the material, the joints and the function the pipe must serve, not on age alone.
Includes break-rate statistics by material from several Swedish cities.

greyLiterature.title: 2017 Infrastructure Report Card: Wastewater (Grade D+)
greyLiterature.organization: American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE)
greyLiterature.summary: ASCE's 2017 grading of US wastewater infrastructure (D+), covering capacity, condition, funding and future need. Cited by Malek Mohammadi et al. (2020) and Li et al. (2023).
keyTakeaways: 56 million more users are expected to connect to centralised treatment by 2032, a 23% increase in demand.
An estimated $271 billion is needed to meet current and future wastewater demands.
Over 800,000 miles of public sewers; as new users connect, older systems must carry more flow.

greyLiterature.title: The Economic Benefits of Investing in Water Infrastructure: How a Failure to Act Would Affect the US Economic Recovery
greyLiterature.organization: American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) and the Value of Water Campaign
greyLiterature.summary: ASCE 'Failure to Act' report on the cost to the US economy of under-investing in drinking water, wastewater and stormwater infrastructure. Cited by Lundberg et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: 2019: water infrastructure needs were $129 billion against $48 billion invested, an $81 billion gap, projected to reach $136 billion a year by 2039.
Closing the gap needs about $109 billion a year for 20 years.
Closing it would create about 800,000 jobs and raise household disposable income by about $2,000.

greyLiterature.title: Sewerage Manual Part 1: Key Planning Issues and Gravity Collection System (3rd edition, with Eurocodes)
greyLiterature.organization: Drainage Services Department (DSD), Hong Kong SAR Government
greyLiterature.summary: Hong Kong's design and planning manual for public gravity sewers: planning and investigation, flow and load estimation, sewer design, manholes, and operation and maintenance. Cited by Lin et al. (2025).
keyTakeaways: Surcharged sewers are undesirable because peak flow recurs daily, grease clogs submerged sewers, and modelling is uncertain.
Existing sewers found surcharged at peak flow, even with freeboard, should be treated as under capacity.
Sewage flows for planning follow EPD's Guidelines for Estimating Sewage Flows (GESF).

greyLiterature.title: Stormwater Drainage Manual: Planning, Design and Management (5th edition)
greyLiterature.organization: Drainage Services Department (DSD), Hong Kong SAR Government
greyLiterature.summary: Hong Kong's stormwater drainage manual: rainfall and sea-level analysis, flood protection standards, runoff estimation, hydraulic analysis, pipe and manhole design, and operation and maintenance. Cited by Lin et al. (2025).
keyTakeaways: Reference for hydraulic analysis and frictional resistance equations for drainage pipes.
Sets design return periods based on flood levels.
Stormwater, not sewage; useful mainly for the hydraulics behind the soft-sensor papers.

greyLiterature.title: IoT as a Digital Enabler of a Hyper-Connected Water Utility
greyLiterature.organization: Sydney Water
greyLiterature.summary: Sydney Water's report (Water e-Journal 4(3), Australian Water Association) on its IoT pilot, including sewer blockage and overflow detection with about 330 sensors in Liverpool, NSW. Cited by Drenoyanis et al. (2022).
keyTakeaways: Three sewer sensor types were deployed: level switches, ultrasonic level sensors and flow sensors; 15 sensor/transmitter models were tested over LoRa and NB-IoT.
Initial placement rule of thumb: a level switch every 3rd access chamber, an analogue level sensor every 30th and a flow sensor every 200th, then refined with business rules.
Sydney Water states there is no generally accepted rule for how many chambers to monitor or which technology to use.

steps.citation: Prackwieser, C., Cash, D. & Wassell, M. (2019). IoT as a digital enabler of a hyper-connected water utility. Water e-Journal 4(3), Australian Water Association. https://doi.org/10.21139/wej.2019.015
steps.intro: Sydney Water's Customer Hub wanted to detect service faults before customers do.
steps.methods: IoT pilot across five use cases, testing devices and networks against an evaluation framework.
steps.scope: Sydney Water water and wastewater assets; sewer use cases in the Liverpool area.
steps.usefulness: A real Australian utility's sensor mix and spacing rule. Directly answers Vineeth's question about which sensor and how far apart.
steps.limitations: Pilot results; the spacing rule is a starting heuristic, not optimised.
steps.conclusions: IoT is viable for sewer monitoring, but challenges include water ingress, gases, rodents and poor reception under iron covers.
steps.reflection: A practical baseline to compare our placement method against: blanket spacing (every 3rd/30th/200th chamber) versus placement at capacity-limiting pipes.

greyLiterature.title: Wipes in Sewer Blockage Study: Final Report
greyLiterature.organization: Water UK (with Defra and EDANA); press release by Severn Trent Water
greyLiterature.summary: UK study of 54 sewer blockages, funded by Water UK, Defra and EDANA. Severn Trent's press release 'New proof that flushing wipes is a major cause of sewer blockages' (2017), cited by Ninh et al. (2026), reports this study.
keyTakeaways: Wipes made up about 93% of blockage material; baby wipes were over 75% by weight of identifiable products.
Products designed to be flushed were under 1% of blockage material.
The UK has about 300,000 sewer blockages a year, costing about £100 million.

greyLiterature.title: MCERTS Performance Standards and Test Procedures for Continuous Water Monitoring Equipment, Part 3: Water Flowmeters (Version 4)
greyLiterature.organization: Environment Agency (England)
greyLiterature.summary: The UK certification standard for water flowmeters, including velocity-area and level-based instruments. Cited by Crowley et al. (2025). The 2020 PDF has been withdrawn: in August 2026 the scheme was replaced by two parts (open channel; closed conduit) based on EN 17694:2023. The link points to the current version.
keyTakeaways: Current Part 1 (open channel instruments) applies to sewers flowing part-full.
Level sensor classes: bias ±0.1% (Class 1), ±0.3% (Class 2), ±1% (Class 3).
Integrated velocity-area instruments: bias ±1.5%, ±4% and ±6.5% for Classes 1–3.

greyLiterature.title: A Guide to Short Term Flow Surveys of Sewer Systems
greyLiterature.organization: WRc (Water Research Centre), UK
greyLiterature.summary: WRc guide (132 pages) to planning and running short-term sewer flow surveys, processing the data and reporting, used to verify hydraulic models of existing sewers. Still a reference for UK flow-survey practice. Cited by Crowley et al. (2025). Not openly available.
keyTakeaways: The industry method for calibrating and verifying sewer hydraulic models against measured flows.
Covers survey planning, field work, data processing and the final report.
Relevant when SA Water data arrives and Sim 2.5 needs calibration.

greyLiterature.title: Sewerage Rehabilitation Manual (now the Sewerage Risk Management website)
greyLiterature.organization: WRc (Water Research Centre), UK
greyLiterature.summary: WRc's Sewerage Rehabilitation Manual, first published in 1980, became the base for sewer condition assessment protocols worldwide. The 4th edition was developed into the online Sewerage Risk Management (SRM) site, funded by eleven UK sewerage utilities with Defra and Ofwat support. Cited by Malek Mohammadi et al. (2020) and Lundberg et al. (2026). Subscription access.
keyTakeaways: The origin of WRc condition grading; condition models typically grade pipes from 1 (new) to 5 (failed).
Covers rehabilitation planning and sewer renovation.
Most condition-prediction studies reviewed by Malek Mohammadi et al. use WRc or PACP grading.

greyLiterature.title: D1.2 Review of Sewer Deterioration Models (SEMA project)
greyLiterature.organization: Kompetenzzentrum Wasser Berlin (KWB)
greyLiterature.summary: Kley & Caradot's review of sewer deterioration models for the SEMA project (Asset Management Strategies for Sewer Systems), covering deterministic, statistical and artificial-intelligence approaches. Cited by Malek Mohammadi et al. (2020). The KWB site could not be reached when this entry was added; check the link.
keyTakeaways: Groups deterioration models into deterministic, statistical and AI-based.
Background for choosing a simple, explainable risk weighting over data-hungry models.

greyLiterature.title: Analysis of Defects in 180 km of Pipe Sewers in Southern Water Authority (TRRL Research Report 172)
greyLiterature.organization: Transport and Road Research Laboratory (TRRL), UK, with Southern Water Authority
greyLiterature.summary: O'Reilly, Rosbrook, Cox & McCloskey's analysis of defects found in 180 km of sewers in the Southern Water Authority area. An early large utility dataset on sewer condition factors. Cited by Malek Mohammadi et al. (2020). Not openly available.
keyTakeaways: One of the early large utility datasets used in sewer condition-factor research.
From the predecessor of Southern Water, where Vineeth worked.

greyLiterature.title: Kortbedömning av TV-inspekterade avloppsledningar (Evaluation of TV-Inspected Sewer Pipes), VA-Forsk Report 1994-12
greyLiterature.organization: VA-Forsk / Svenskt Vatten (Swedish Water & Wastewater Association)
greyLiterature.summary: Nilsson & Stahre's Swedish system for quickly grading CCTV-inspected gravity sewers, giving an operational grade and a pipe grade from weighted defects, to help municipalities plan renewal. Cited by Lundberg et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: Separates operational (blockage-type) grades from structural pipe grades.
Still used as a framework for Swedish CCTV grading.

greyLiterature.title: Hong Kong Conduit Condition Evaluation Codes (HKCCEC), 2009 version
greyLiterature.organization: Utility Training Institute (UTI), Hong Kong
greyLiterature.summary: Hong Kong's code for evaluating conduit condition from CCTV and man-entry surveys. The 2009 version added a Structural Performance Grade. Later issued as the Conduit Condition Evaluation Codes (5th edition, 2019). Cited by Ma et al. (2026). No open copy found.
keyTakeaways: The Hong Kong grading code referenced in Ma et al. (2026)'s review of AI sewer condition models.
Shows why Hong Kong condition thresholds should not be applied directly to Adelaide.

greyLiterature.title: Analysing Sewer Flow Patterns to Detect Blockages and Overflows (OzWater'21, Adelaide)
greyLiterature.organization: Sydney Water
greyLiterature.summary: Januszek, Rahman & Cheung's OzWater'21 paper on detecting overflows and blockages upstream of sewage pumping stations from pump-station data. Described in, and cited by, Drenoyanis et al. (2022). The conference paper is not openly available; the link is the Drenoyanis article that summarises it.
keyTakeaways: Compares wet-well inflow rates and pump run times with historical diurnal patterns and flags abnormally low inflow.
Works only if the lost flow is large relative to normal pump-station inflow; small chokes look like natural variation.
An 'identify before prevent' method using data SA Water already holds (pump-station SCADA).

greyLiterature.title: Keeping Our Sewers Healthy
greyLiterature.organization: SA Water
greyLiterature.summary: SA Water's public page on blockages and overflows: what should and should not be flushed, fats and oils, its sewer cleaning program and smart sensor trials. Cited by Ninh et al. (2026).
keyTakeaways: In 2022-23, 'unflushables' caused more than 3,500 blockages across metropolitan Adelaide.
Wet wipes and feminine hygiene products are about 90% of material removed from blocked sewers; they tangle in tree roots.
More than two-thirds of overflows occur inside customers' properties. SA Water cleans a 9,000 km network and is trialling smart sewer sensors.

greyLiterature.title: What's Really Going Down Adelaide's Sewers?
greyLiterature.organization: South Australian Government (We Are SA) with SA Water
greyLiterature.summary: SA Government news article on record wet-wipe blockages in Adelaide's sewers and unusual items found by SA Water crews. Cited by Ninh et al. (2026). The page blocks automated access; figures are taken from search summaries and should be checked on the page.
keyTakeaways: Reports 1,667 wet-wipe blockages in Adelaide by mid-November 2024, beating the 2022 record of 1,344.
Context for SA Water's blockage problem, which is separate from the growth use case.

greyLiterature.title: DSD Sustainability Report 2019-20: Innovation for Sustainability of Water Purification and Flood Protection
greyLiterature.organization: Drainage Services Department (DSD), Hong Kong SAR Government
greyLiterature.summary: DSD's annual sustainability report (GRI Standards) on its sewerage and drainage work in 2019-20, including innovative maintenance technology. Cited by Ma et al. (2025).
keyTakeaways: Hong Kong utility context for the Ma et al. sewer-condition dataset.
Includes remote-controlled desilting robots for confined, submerged drains.

greyLiterature.title: Sewage Strategy
greyLiterature.organization: Drainage Services Department (DSD), Hong Kong SAR Government
greyLiterature.summary: DSD's overview of Hong Kong's sewerage strategy: network size, Sewerage Master Plans and the Harbour Area Treatment Scheme. Cited by Ma et al. (2025).
keyTakeaways: About 93% of the population is served by about 1,700 km of public sewers and around 300 pumping stations and treatment facilities.
Older urban sewerage was not upgraded for later development; Sewerage Master Plans upgrade 16 catchments one at a time.
A growth-driven capacity upgrade programme at city scale.
